q: You are issuing lifejackets for a coastal passage between the Cyclades. Which rating do you give each adult as a minimum?
o: Any rating, if it fits
why: 150 N suits coastal and offshore sailing; 50 N is a buoyancy aid, 100 N is for sheltered water.

q: The charter boat has both automatic and manual gas lifejackets. You give the automatics to the crew who will be on deck at night. Why?
a: They inflate even if the wearer is knocked out
o: They give more buoyancy than the manual ones
They never need a service or a re-arm kit
They can be worn without a crotch strap
why: Automatic inflation works on immersion — a stunned wearer cannot pull the toggle.

q: A crew member is ready to go on deck wearing her lifejacket like this. What do you change?
a: Tighten the waist belt, fasten the crotch strap
o: Move it under the foul-weather jacket instead
Nothing — a fastened waist buckle is enough
Partly inflate it so it is ready to float
why: Without a snug belt and crotch strap an inflated jacket rides up over the face.

fig.title: Lifejacket check
lines: Waist buckle done up, but loose
Crotch strap tucked inside the jacket

q: You have fallen in during a rough night passage and waves keep breaking over your face. What do you do with your lifejacket?
a: Pull its sprayhood down over your face
o: Let some air out so you sit lower
Take it off and hold it in front of you
Unclip the crotch strap to turn more easily
why: The sprayhood keeps breaking water out of your mouth and nose.

q: At the charter base you check the gas lifejackets before signing for them. What do you look at?
a: Cylinder tight and unfired, indicators green
o: Pull each toggle once to test the cylinder
Only that each one has a whistle and light
Only the colour, so they show up in the water
why: A loose or fired cylinder means no inflation; firing one to test it leaves it useless.

q: You are checking the safety gear against your crew list. What do you need before sailing?
a: A child's lifejacket sized for her weight
o: An adult jacket with the straps pulled tight
A swimming ring for when she is on deck
Nothing, if she stays in the cockpit
why: Lifejackets are sized by weight; an adult jacket slips straight off a child.

q: You are putting on foul-weather gear for the night watch. Where does the lifejacket go?
a: Over the jacket, as the outer layer
o: Under the jacket, to keep it dry
Clipped to the binnacle within reach
Under the fleece, next to the body
why: Worn underneath, the bladder cannot inflate properly and may crush your chest.

q: You are coming up from below to start your watch. When do you clip on?
a: Before you leave the companionway
o: Once you are sitting at the helm
Only if you go forward of the mast
When the skipper tells you to clip on
why: Clip to a strong point from the hatch so you are never on deck unattached.

q: You are on the foredeck on a two-legged tether and need to move from the jackstay to the strong point at the mast. How do you change over?
a: Clip the second hook on, then unclip the first
o: Unclip, step across quickly, then clip on again
Unclip and hold on to the mast with both hands
Stay on the jackstay and stretch across
why: Always one hook attached: make the new clip before you release the old one.

q: You are rigging jackstays at the base before a night crossing. How do you lead them?
a: Bow to cockpit on deck, inboard and taut
o: Along the guardrails at waist height
Outside the shrouds, along the toerail
From the mast to the pulpit, slack
why: Tight, inboard jackstays stop a tethered crew reaching the water; guardrails are not strong points.

q: You are alone on watch at 03:00 in a calm sea while everyone else sleeps. Do you clip on?
a: Yes, for the whole watch
o: No — the sea is calm
Only if you leave the cockpit
Only if the wind rises above 20 knots
why: Alone at night nobody would see you go over: clip on whatever the weather.

q: You will helm this boat at night with a 2 m tether. Where do you clip on?
a: Where the tether cannot reach the open transom
o: To the strong point nearest the transom edge
To the guardrail wire beside the helm seat
Anywhere — any tether keeps you aboard
why: A tether only helps if it is too short to let you reach the water.

fig.title: Cockpit layout
lines: Strong points: at the hatch and the transom
Helm seat 1.5 m from the stern edge

q: You plan a night crossing on day three of the charter. What do you do about it at check-in?
a: Ask the base for harnesses, tethers and jackstays
o: Nothing — lifejackets are enough at night
Tie spare mooring lines round the crew as tethers
Plan to motor so nobody needs to go forward
why: Without harnesses and jackstays no one can stay attached on deck at night.

q: The liferaft sits in a cradle on the pushpit with a hydrostatic release. The yacht sinks before anyone can launch it. What happens?
a: It is freed at a few metres, floats up and inflates
o: Nothing — it goes down with the yacht
It inflates on deck as soon as it gets wet
It only releases if someone cuts the lashing first
why: The HRU lets the raft float free; the taut painter fires the inflation, then a weak link breaks.

q: You are checking the liferaft before a week on charter. What do you do?
a: Ask the base for a raft that is in service
o: Accept it — a sealed raft lasts for years
Open the canister to check it yourself
Inflate it on the pontoon to test it works
why: An out-of-date raft may not inflate; only an approved station services one.

q: During check-in you find the valise liferaft at the bottom of the cockpit locker, under fenders, lines and the outboard fuel. What do you do?
a: Restow it on top so it can be lifted out fast
o: Leave it — it is dry and protected down there
Move it to the forepeak, out of the way
Lash it down hard at the bottom of the locker
why: A liferaft must be reachable and launchable in seconds.

q: You find the canister raft on the coachroof like this. What do you do?
a: Remove the extra ropes so it can float free
o: Leave them — now the raft can never be lost
Add a padlock so it cannot be stolen
Untie the painter from the cradle as well
why: Extra lashings defeat the hydrostatic release; the raft would sink with the yacht.

fig.title: Check-in: coachroof
lines: Base has added two rope lashings over it

q: Which extinguisher do you reach for?
a: Dry powder or foam
o: A bucket of sea water
The deck-wash hose
A wet towel to beat it out
why: Burning fuel is a Class B fire: water spreads it, powder or foam smothers it.

fig.title: Aft deck
lines: Petrol spilt filling the outboard tank
Now burning in a pool on deck

q: You are first to the chart table. What is your plan?
a: Isolate the batteries, then use CO2 or powder
o: Spray foam into the panel at once, then isolate
Throw a bucket of water over the panel
Open the panel to find the burning wire first
why: Cut the power so it cannot re-ignite; never water or foam on live electrics.

fig.title: Chart table
lines: Smoke from behind the switch panel

q: You are at the helm when this starts. How do you fight it?
a: Stop engine and fuel, discharge through the fire port
o: Lift the engine box and spray straight at the flames
Keep the engine running so the fan clears the smoke
Open the hatches below to let the smoke out
why: Opening the box feeds the fire with air; the fire port floods the space while it stays shut.

fig.title: Motoring
lines: Engine alarm, smoke from the engine box
Small hole in the box marked FIRE PORT

q: What is wrong with this galley?
a: You must reach over the flames to get the blanket
o: Nothing — it is as close to the fire as possible
It should be inside a locker to keep it dry
It belongs in the cockpit, ready for deck fires
why: Mount the blanket near the galley but to one side, so you never lean over a burning pan.

q: How do you put this fire out?
a: Douse it thoroughly with water
o: Use only CO2 — never water below
Open the forehatch to clear the smoke
Shut the cabin door and let it burn out
why: Fabric and foam are Class A: water cools and soaks them so they do not re-ignite.

fig.title: Forecabin
lines: Candle knocked over onto a cushion
Galley tap and buckets close by

q: How do the two in the forecabin get out?
a: Through the forehatch onto the foredeck
o: Through the saloon, fast, with wet towels
Shut the cabin door and wait inside
Through the companionway once it clears
why: Brief everyone on the escape hatches; never go through a fire to reach the main exit.

fig.title: Fire in the saloon
lines: Two crew asleep in the forecabin

q: Heeled on starboard tack, the cook wants to heat soup for the crew. How do you set up the galley?
a: Gimbals free, pan clamps on, cook braced in a strap
o: Lock the gimbals so the stove stays level
Stand on the low side, right in front of the stove
Fill the pan well up so it sits steadier
why: The stove swings level on its gimbals; scalds come from pans falling onto a cook on the low side.

q: You are checking where the gas alarm sensor is fitted. Where should it be?
a: Low down, near the bilge below the cooker
o: High up, near the deckhead above the cooker
Beside the companionway at head height
In the cockpit, next to the gas bottle
why: LPG is heavier than air: it sinks and collects in the bilge.

q: You run the daily gas check. What does this tell you?
a: A leak — shut the bottle and do not use the gas
o: All normal — gas is flowing to the cooker
The bottle is nearly empty and needs changing
The regulator is working just as it should
why: With every appliance off no gas should flow; bubbles mean it is escaping somewhere.

fig.title: Gas locker
lines: Press the bubble tester: a steady stream

q: You are about to leave the boat for dinner ashore. What do you do?
a: Switch the gas solenoid off
o: Leave it — the cooker knobs are off
Leave it on, ready for breakfast
Turn it off only before you sleep
why: The solenoid is open only while cooking; a closed valve cannot feed a leak.

lines: Crew going ashore for the evening

q: You have just connected a new gas bottle in the locker. How do you check the joint?
a: Brush soapy water on it, watch for bubbles
o: Hold a lighter near it to look for a flame
Sniff it closely for any smell of gas
Light the cooker and listen at the locker
why: Soapy water shows the smallest leak without any flame.

q: You are told this over breakfast. What do you suspect, and what do you do?
a: Carbon monoxide — fresh air and medical advice
o: Seasickness — a tablet each and lie them down
Dehydration — plenty of water and back to bed
Food poisoning — let them sleep it off below
why: Headache and nausea in a cabin near an exhaust is CO until proved otherwise.

fig.title: Morning after rafting up
lines: Motor yacht alongside: generator all night
Its exhaust beside your aft cabin port
Two crew from that cabin: headache, nausea

q: The alarm wakes you. How do you respond?
a: Get everyone into fresh air, find the source
o: Ignore it — you would smell a real leak
Reset it and check it in the morning
Take the battery out and go back to sleep
why: Carbon monoxide has no smell; sleepers can be poisoned before they notice symptoms.

lines: No smell, nobody feels ill yet

q: An hour out of Lavrio a crew member feels queasy. What do you suggest?
a: Stay on deck, take the helm, watch the horizon
o: Go below and lie down in the forecabin
Read the pilot book to take her mind off it
Eat a large, rich lunch to settle her stomach
why: Fresh air, the horizon and a job help; the forecabin has the most motion.

q: At night a seasick crew member needs to be sick. Where?
a: Leeward side, clipped on, someone watching
o: Windward rail, clipped on, so it blows clear
Alone at the stern, out of everyone's sight
At the leeward rail, unclipped for comfort
why: Seasick crew are a classic overboard risk: leeward, clipped on and in sight.

q: A crew member who gets seasick asks when to take her tablets for tomorrow's crossing. What do you tell her?
a: Before you leave, as the packet says
o: As soon as you start to feel sick
Only if the wind is above Force 5
Halfway across, if it gets rough
why: Seasickness tablets need time to work; once vomiting starts they barely stay down.

q: You are skipper on this passage. How do you treat this crew member?
a: As serious: frequent sips, consider diverting
o: Normal seasickness — she will adapt by tomorrow
A large glass of water in one go, then sleep
Keep her on the helm to take her mind off it
why: Prolonged vomiting causes dangerous dehydration; give sips often and seek help early.

fig.title: Passage, day 2
lines: Drowsy, dark urine, dizzy on standing

q: A crew member calls you to the cockpit. What is wrong, and what do you do?
a: Heatstroke: shade, cool with water and air, get help
o: Heat exhaustion: rest below with a cold beer
Sunburn: after-sun cream and a sleep in the cabin
Chill from the swim: wrap them up in a blanket
why: Hot dry skin and confusion mean heatstroke — cool fast and get medical help.

fig.title: Anchored, 14:00
lines: Crew member swam, then slept in the sun
Hot, red, dry skin; very hot to touch

q: How do you look after this crew member?
a: Shade, rest, sips of water with rehydration salts
o: Strong coffee to perk them up, then back to work
Keep them working and make them drink at dinner
Wrap them in a foil blanket and let them sleep
why: Heat exhaustion: a cool place, fluids and salts — before it becomes heatstroke.

fig.title: Motoring, no wind
lines: Crew member pale and sweating heavily
Dizzy, headache, cramps in the legs

q: How do you plan the day for the crew?
a: Bimini up, regular water, hats and sunscreen
o: Cold beer through the day instead of water
Hourly swims, so drinking matters less
Sprayhood down for the breeze, hats off
why: Shade, steady drinking and sun cover prevent sunburn, dehydration and heat illness.

q: You fall in on an April delivery trip. The water is 15 °C and you are gasping uncontrollably. What do you do for the first minute?
a: Lean back, float and let your breathing settle
o: Swim hard for the boat straight away
Kick off your boots and pull off your jacket
Shout and wave continuously so they hear you
why: Cold-water shock passes in about a minute; float until you control your breathing.

q: You come up to check on the watch. What do you do for the helm?
a: Relieve them: dry clothes below, warm sweet drink
o: A tot of brandy to warm up, then back on watch
Rub their arms and legs hard to get blood flowing
Keep them helming so they stay active and warm
why: Early hypothermia: shelter, dry insulation and warm sweet drinks; no alcohol.

q: You are the nearest crew member. What is your first aid?
a: Cool it under running water for 20 minutes
o: Spread butter on it to soothe the pain
Pop the blisters so the skin can heal
Hold ice straight on the skin until numb
why: Cool running water for 20 minutes limits the damage; no ice, fats or bursting blisters.

fig.title: Galley, under way
lines: Kettle tipped over in a wave

q: You have cooled a scald on a crew member's hand for 20 minutes. How do you cover it?
a: A loose layer of cling film, no creams
o: A fluffy cotton-wool pad, taped down
A tight bandage to stop the swelling
Antiseptic cream under a large plaster
why: Cling film laid on loosely protects a burn and does not stick to it.

q: You grab the first-aid kit. What do you do first for this wound?
a: Press firmly on it with a clean pad
o: Tie a tourniquet above the wrist
Rinse it in the sea and leave it open
Pull the edges apart to clean it out
why: Firm direct pressure stops most bleeding; a tourniquet is for life-threatening limb bleeding only.

fig.title: Foredeck
lines: Knife slipped while cutting a line

q: How do you manage this casualty?
a: Watch them closely and get medical advice
o: Nothing more — they are awake and talking
Painkillers and let them sleep alone below
A stiff drink to steady them, then carry on
why: Any loss of consciousness needs medical advice; signs of brain injury can appear hours later.

fig.title: Accidental gybe
lines: Boom hit a crew member's head
Knocked out for a few seconds

q: You check on the casualty from the morning. What do you conclude?
a: Serious head injury — get urgent medical help
o: Seasickness — a tablet and some rest below
Tiredness after the shock — let them sleep it off
Dehydration — plenty of fluids and an early night
why: Repeated vomiting, drowsiness and unequal pupils point to pressure on the brain.

fig.title: Later that evening
lines: Hit by the boom four hours ago
One pupil larger than the other

q: You are sailing like this and the boat is rolling. How do you protect the crew?
a: Rig a preventer, keep heads clear of the boom
o: Ease the mainsheet fully and let the boom swing
Let the crew sit up on the coachroof
Steer slightly by the lee to keep the sail full
why: An accidental gybe swings the boom across hard; a preventer holds it.

fig.note: Dead run in a swell, crew in the cockpit

q: Coming stern-to in Hydra, the transom is about to touch the quay. A crew member stretches a foot out to push off. What do you tell her?
a: Keep your feet in — use a roving fender
o: Push off with your hand instead of a foot
Push only once the boat has stopped moving
Sit on the transom and brace with both feet
why: Never put a limb between boat and quay; several tonnes will crush it.

q: A crew member presses the electric winch button to hoist the main while another feeds the halyard. What is the rule?
a: The one pressing watches, ready to stop
o: Press in long bursts so it is over quickly
The feeder keeps a hand close to the drum
Leave the clutch open in case it jams
why: Electric winches crush fingers and break gear; the operator watches and stops at any snag.

q: Weighing anchor, a crew member wants to guide the chain onto the windlass by hand while you press the button. What do you say?
a: Hands clear — signal to me and I will stop
o: Fine, as long as you wear sailing gloves
Fine, but only at slow speed
Hold it on the gypsy with your foot instead
why: A windlass will not stop for fingers; hands and feet stay away from the gypsy.

q: The swimmer seems well again. What do you do?
a: Get her checked by a doctor today
o: Nothing — she's fine now
A hot shower and an early night
Another swim to rebuild her confidence
why: Water in the lungs can cause breathing problems hours later; anyone who inhaled water needs checking.

q: You pull a swimmer from the water. He is unresponsive and not breathing normally. How do you start CPR?
a: Five rescue breaths, then 30 compressions to 2
o: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, compressions first
Hold him upside down to drain the water first
Recovery position and wait for him to breathe
why: Drowning is a lack of oxygen, so CPR starts with five rescue breaths.

q: You reach the casualty. How do you look after him?
a: Recovery position, keep checking the breathing
o: Sit him upright on the cockpit seat to recover
Start chest compressions at once
Splash him with cold water and leave him there
why: Unresponsive but breathing: the recovery position keeps the airway open.

fig.title: Anchored, afternoon
lines: Crew member fainted in the cockpit
Does not respond to your voice

q: Your charter crew are mostly friends of friends. Before sailing, what do you ask them about their health?
a: Conditions, allergies and medicines
o: Nothing — their health is private
Only whether they can swim well
Only whether they get seasick
why: The skipper must know medical needs before a problem happens miles from help.

q: How do you treat the sting?
a: Rinse with sea water, lift tentacles off
o: Rinse with fresh water and rub it dry
Rub wet sand on it to scrape it clean
Pour urine on it to stop the stinging
why: Fresh water and rubbing make the stinging cells fire; rinse with sea water, no rubbing.

fig.title: Swimming off Vis
lines: Crew member stung on the arm
Pieces of tentacle still on the skin

q: What is likely, and how do you treat it?
a: Weever fish — soak the foot in hot water
o: Weever fish — pack the foot in ice
Sea urchin — dig the spine out with a knife
Jellyfish — rinse it with fresh water
why: Weever venom is broken down by heat; water as hot as is bearable, without scalding, eases it.

fig.title: Wading ashore, sandy bay
lines: Sudden, intense pain in the foot
One small puncture, no spines in it

q: What do you do before anyone goes in?
a: Stop the engine and lower the ladder
o: Put the engine in neutral and let them go
Let them jump, lower the ladder later
Keep the engine on, swim from the bow
why: No swimming with the engine running; the ladder goes down before anyone jumps.

q: Your crew want to swim off the stern. What do you rig first?
a: A floating line streamed astern
o: A line from the bow to the shore
Nothing — the anchor holds the boat still
The tender, tied up alongside the bow
why: A trailing line gives a tired swimmer something to grab before being carried away.

fig.note: At anchor · wind 15 kn · current setting south

q: A crew member wants to swim from the yacht to the beach. What do you insist on?
a: A bright tow float, clear of the tender route
o: The tender route, as it is the shortest way
Nothing — rib drivers will see her head
Going at dusk, when the water is calmer
why: A swimmer's head is almost invisible to a rib driver; a bright float and a clear route save lives.

fig.note: Y: your yacht, 300 m off the beach

q: After dinner aboard with wine, two crew want a moonlit swim off the stern. What do you say?
a: No swimming after drinking or in the dark
o: Fine, as long as they stay near the ladder
Fine, if they wear masks and fins
Fine, if the deck lights are on
why: Alcohol slows reactions, and in the dark nobody sees a swimmer in trouble.

q: How do you get them ashore?
a: Two trips
o: One trip — it is calm and close
One trip, two sitting on the tubes
One trip, the heaviest at the bow
why: The builder's plate is the limit; overloaded tenders swamp and capsize.

fig.title: Tender
lines: 6 crew want to go ashore for dinner
Calm bay, 200 m to the quay

q: What do you need for the trip back to the yacht?
a: A torch to show, lifejackets on, a sober driver
o: Nothing — the anchor lights will show the way
Full speed, to spend less time on the water
All torches off to keep your night vision
why: An unlit tender is invisible to other tenders; darkness and drink cause many accidents.

fig.title: Back from the taverna
lines: Crew have had wine with dinner

q: You are passing the outboard down from the pushpit into the tender. How do you do it?
a: Safety line on until it is clamped and secured
o: Carry it down the ladder in one hand
Drop it on the floor and clamp it on later
Hand it across without a line — it is quicker
why: Outboards are easily dropped overboard; keep a line on until clamped and secured.

q: You are about to start the outboard. What do you do before pulling the cord?
a: Neutral, and wait until the swimmers are clear
o: Pull it now — the tender is tied to the yacht
Start it in forward so it moves off quickly
Ask the swimmers to hold on to the transom
why: A propeller turning near swimmers causes terrible injuries; neutral and clear water first.

fig.title: Starting the outboard
lines: Two crew swimming next to it

q: You are taking the crew ashore. What must be in the tender?
a: Oars, a bailer and a phone in a dry bag
o: Only the fuel tank — the engine is new
Nothing extra, the trip is short
A spare anchor and chain for the yacht
why: If the outboard fails in an offshore wind you drift out to sea; carry oars and a way to call.

fig.title: Going ashore
lines: Wind 15 kn blowing off the beach

q: You buy a 5-litre can of petrol for the outboard in Fethiye. Where do you stow it?
a: On deck or in a locker draining overboard
o: In the bilge, where it stays cool and dark
In the engine bay beside the diesel
In the forepeak locker with the fenders
why: Petrol vapour, like gas, sinks and can explode below; keep it outside the hull.

q: At night a male crew member heads to the stern rail to relieve himself over the side. What do you tell him?
a: Use the heads below instead
o: Clip on to the guardrail first
Do it at the bow instead
Fine, as long as the sea is calm
why: Relieving yourself over the rail is a classic cause of falling overboard, above all at night.

q: The horseshoe is thrown and a spotter is pointing. What do you do at the plotter?
a: Press the MOB button to mark the spot
o: Write the position down in the log book
Switch the display over to radar
Zoom out to find the nearest port
why: The MOB button fixes the position at once — vital if you lose sight of the casualty.

q: You find this on your check-in walk round. What do you do?
a: Cut the ties and clear the danbuoy line
o: Leave them — the ties stop theft in port
Add more ties so nothing blows off at sea
Stow both in the cockpit locker for now
why: Throwable gear must leave the boat in seconds: no ties, no tangles.

fig.title: Check-in: pushpit
lines: Held on with three cable ties
Danbuoy line tangled round its flag

q: You are going forward in daylight to check the anchor locker, the boat pitching in a short sea. How do you move?
a: Windward side, low, one hand always holding
o: Leeward side, sheltered by the sails
Upright and quick, to spend less time there
Along the outside of the guardrails
why: One hand for yourself, one for the boat; to windward you fall into the boat, not over the side.

q: What is your rule?
a: Whoever helms or keeps watch stays off alcohol
o: Anyone may drink if the skipper stays sober
Two beers each is fine for everyone aboard
Fine to drink once the sails are up
why: Alcohol slows reactions and raises the risk of going overboard; helm and watch stay sober.

fig.title: Lunch stop, Hvar
lines: Crew have had a few beers

q: How do you plan the night?
a: Set watches so everyone sleeps, including you
o: Stay on deck all night yourself to be safe
Everyone stays up — it is only one night
Sort out watches once people get tired
why: A tired skipper makes poor decisions; a watch system gives everyone rest.

fig.title: Overnight passage
lines: Crew of 6, you the only skipper

q: How do you split the watches?
a: One led by you, one by Anna, novices shared
o: You and Anna together, the novices together
Novices on deck, you two asleep below
Everyone on deck together all night
why: Each watch needs an experienced leader; novices learn and are never left alone.

fig.title: Crew for the night crossing
lines: Ben, Chris, Dana: first night sail

q: You are at the helm. How do you handle the crew?
a: Tell them what's happening and the plan
o: Say nothing so as not to alarm them
Tell them it will soon die down
Send everyone below until it is over
why: Crew who know the plan stay calmer and can help; uncertainty breeds fear.

fig.title: Halfway across
lines: Wind up from F4 to F6

q: In your safety briefing, who do you show how to stop the boat, use the VHF and start the MOB drill?
a: At least one other crew member
o: Nobody — the skipper does all that
Only the person who booked the boat
Whoever happens to be helming
why: If the skipper goes overboard or is hurt, someone else must be able to take charge.

q: Your rule is lifejackets on deck at night. A crew member says they are for beginners and refuses. What do you do?
a: Insist — the skipper's rule stands
o: Let him decide for himself
Let him off if he is a strong swimmer
Let him wear it, unfastened
why: The skipper is responsible for everyone aboard and sets the safety rules.

q: You review the rota after dinner. What do you change?
a: Pair him up or take him off the solo watch
o: Nothing — the tablets stop him being sick
Give him strong coffee and keep the rota
Let the autopilot steer while he dozes
why: Many seasickness tablets cause drowsiness; a sleepy lone watchkeeper is a danger.

q: You must decide on tonight's landfall. What do you do?
a: Stay offshore, rest in turns, enter at dawn
o: Go in now, before you get even more tired
Go in now with everyone on deck as lookouts
Feel your way in and anchor at the entrance
why: Fatigue and an unknown, unlit entry don't mix; with sea room, wait for daylight.

fig.title: Approaching Turkey
lines: You have been up since 06:00; now 23:00
Crew tired, light wind, plenty of sea room

q: When do you reef?
a: Before leaving the harbour
o: When the wind reaches F6
When the boat starts heeling hard
Halfway, once you see how it goes
why: Reef early: it is easy in shelter and hard once you are overpowered.

q: What do you do below before leaving?
a: Lock floorboards and lockers, stow heavy items
o: Leave everything out so it is close to hand
Open the hatches for fresh air below
Pile the heavy bags on the saloon table
why: In a knockdown loose heavy items become missiles and floorboards fly.

fig.title: Before the crossing
lines: Floorboards loose, tins in an open locker

q: You expect six hours of rough beating. What do you do about food?
a: Make sandwiches and fill flasks before you go
o: Cook a full hot meal once it gets rough
Skip food altogether until you arrive
Plan a hot fry-up halfway across the passage
why: Cooking in rough weather is hard and risky; hungry crew tire and get seasick faster.

q: What do you do with the washboards?
a: Fit the lower ones, keep the rest at hand
o: Leave them out so crew get below quickly
Fit them only once water has come below
Leave them stowed in the locker below
why: If a wave fills the cockpit, the washboards stop it pouring below.

fig.title: Running before a big sea
lines: Two crew in the cockpit, one below

q: Your novice crew are due to cross 25 miles of open water tomorrow. What do you do?
a: Stay in harbour until it passes
o: Leave at first light, before it builds
Go, and reef once it gets rough
Go under engine and motor through
why: The best heavy-weather tactic for a charter crew is not to be out in it.

fig.note: Tomorrow: NW F7 from dawn, all day

q: Conditions are as shown. What do you decide?
a: Bear away for the sheltered bay
o: Press on — it is the plan
Send the sick crew below and carry on
Start the engine and motor into it
why: A tired, sick crew is a hazard; turn for shelter while you still can.

fig.title: Beating to windward
lines: Wind F6 on the nose, 18 miles to go
Two of five crew seasick, one exhausted

q: Your crew are going on night watch for the first time. How do you protect their night vision?
a: Red lights below, dimmed screens
o: White cabin lights on for safety
Bright plotter screen for detail
Head torch on full beam on deck
why: Night vision takes many minutes to come back after white light.

q: You are on watch with the skipper asleep below. What do you do?
a: Wake the skipper now
o: Wait until it is closer
Shine a torch at it
Alter course quietly
why: A steady bearing means risk of collision: call the skipper early, never late.

q: At night you need to go forward to clear a fouled furling line. What do you do first?
a: Tell the helm, clip on, take a head torch
o: Go quietly so you wake nobody below
Unclip so you can move faster forward
Go without a light to keep night vision
why: Nobody goes forward at night without the helm knowing, clipped on and with a light.

q: You are finishing the grab bag. Which item is most worth adding?
a: A handheld VHF in a waterproof pouch
o: Paper charts of the whole cruising area
The boat's toolbox and spare fuses
A saucepan and a gas canister
why: In a liferaft, a way to talk to rescuers matters more than anything else.

fig.title: Grab bag so far
lines: Copies of passports and boat papers

q: Where do you keep the grab bag during a charter week?
a: By the companionway, known to all
o: Under the forecabin bunk, out of the way
In the cockpit locker under the lines
In the skipper's cabin, locked
why: In an emergency you have seconds; the grab bag must be on the way out.

q: You are packing drinking water for the grab bag. How?
a: Small bottles, not quite full
o: One full 5-litre can
Glass bottles, to keep it fresh
None — the liferaft has enough
why: Part-filled small bottles float if dropped and are easy to share out.

q: You are checking the fire gear at the base. What do you do?
a: Have it replaced before you leave
o: Accept it — red is normal for powder
Shake it to bring the needle back
Sign for it, report it at the end
why: A needle in the red means low pressure; the extinguisher may not work.

q: You count the lifejackets at check-in. What do you do?
a: Get two more from the base before sailing
o: Share them — not all are on deck at once
Sail; the two best swimmers go without
Use cockpit cushions for the other two
why: There must be a lifejacket of the right size for every person aboard.
